chapters.title: Te reo Māori greetings — kia ora and tēnā koe
chapters.content: Kia ora is a versatile greeting in te reo Māori, commonly used like hello, hi or thanks depending on the situation. Tēnā koe is a greeting addressed to one person. Tēnā kōrua addresses two people, and tēnā koutou addresses three or more. These are introductory examples; always respect the local context and tikanga.
chapters.source: Original project explanation checked against University of Auckland greetings guide: https://www.auckland.ac.nz/en/on-campus/life-on-campus/maori-life-on-campus/revitalising-te-reo-maori/kuputaka/greetings-and-sign-offs.html

chapters.title: Te reo Māori farewells — haere rā and e noho rā
chapters.content: In a common farewell exchange, haere rā is said to someone who is leaving; e noho rā is said to someone who is staying. Ka kite anō means see you again. The distinction matters, and the best expression can depend on situation and relationship.
chapters.source: Original project explanation checked against University of Waikato pronunciation and greeting guidance: https://www.waikato.ac.nz/int/students/maori/pronunciation/

chapters.title: Te reo Māori written vowels — macrons and pronunciation
chapters.content: Written te reo Māori uses macrons, such as ā, ē, ī, ō and ū, to indicate long vowels. Correct macrons can distinguish words and meanings. A text reference pack does not provide reliable spoken pronunciation; audio lessons and speaker-reviewed speech capabilities would need their own authorised resources and testing.
